units.translation: ἤγουν ἀμφὶ τῷ Ξέρξῃ · ὀφθαλμὸν γὰρ ἐκεῖνον καλεῖ [that is, around Xerxes; for he calls him an eye]

where M has οὔφεις [serpent], which Porson corrected, following Turnebus, who had written ὄφις [serpent]. It is written with a diphthong in M, because although it is sometimes shortened, it is generally long: on which see Thes. vol. 5 p. 2454. Photius p. 363, 27 ὄφις: ἐκτείνουσι κατὰ τὸ ἑνικόν [they lengthen it in the singular], which Attic measure Herodian noted in Cram. Anecd. Oxon. vol. 3 p. 298 on the noun όφις [serpent] and some others, and Aristocles in his work on dialects says that the Attics lengthen it.
and the encircling vessel is dashed to the ground by the coils of serpents
ὄφις: ἐκτείνουσι κατὰ τὸ ἑνικόν [serpent: they lengthen it in the singular]
Ἀριστοκλῆς δὲ ἐν τῷ περὶ διαλέκτων φησὶν Ἀττικοὺς ἐκτείνειν [And Aristocles in his work on dialects says that the Attics lengthen it]
for having incurred a penalty for robbery and theft
It is an epic particle, which besides Aeschylus Sophocles used once, El. 225, never Euripides.
for he was king, as long as he lived
to accompany them, until he goes under the earth
in the verses of an interpolator
moving a bright eyebrow in the darkness
which is properly said of leading streams or waters, improperly used for μεταφέρω [I transfer], as Hesychius explains
as the report was channeled to the house

this I added. Thus I corrected for νώτοις ὑποστενάζει [he groans under the burden on his shoulders]. The same verb seems to be used of Atlas sustaining the sky on his shoulders in Euripides at the beginning of Ion: ῎Ατλας ὁ χολκέοισι νώτοις οὐρανὸν, θεῶν παλαιὸν οἶκον, ἐκτρίβων, θεῶν μιᾶς ἔφυσε Μαῖαν [Atlas, wearing out the sky with his bronze shoulders, the ancient home of the gods, begot Maia from one of the gods], in manifestly interpolated words, which should be corrected as ῎Ατλας ὁ χαλκόνωτος οὐρανὸν, θεῶν | παλαιὸν οἶκον, ἐκ τριῶν μιᾶς | θεῶν ἔφυσε Μαῖαν [Atlas, bronze-backed, begot Maia from one of the three gods, the ancient home of the gods], as I showed in the Preface to the Leipzig edition of Sophocles, 1867, p. V.
I will sustain an unenviable watch
the strength of the earth and the heavenly pole he groans, sustaining on his shoulders
νώτοις ὑποστενάζει [he groans under the burden on his shoulders]

῎Ατλας ὁ χολκέοισι νώτοις οὐρανὸν, θεῶν παλαιὸν οἶκον, ἐκτρίβων, θεῶν μιᾶς ἔφυσε Μαῖαν [Atlas, wearing out the sky with his bronze shoulders, the ancient home of the gods, begot Maia from one of the gods]
῎Ατλας ὁ χαλκόνωτος οὐρανὸν, θεῶν | παλαιὸν οἶκον, ἐκ τριῶν μιᾶς | θεῶν ἔφυσε Μαῖαν [Atlas, bronze-backed, begot Maia from one of the three gods, the ancient home of the gods]
he invented linen-winged vehicles of sailors
without vehicles and the luxury of former times
κἀχερουσίας [and of Acherousia] Blomfield, as Casaubon for ὄχθους [banks].
